subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Birth of Crash Test Programs
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Birth of Crash Test Programs.

hook.text: Until the 1970s, car buyers had no way to compare how safe one model was versus another.

buildup.text: Automakers tested cars internally but kept every result secret from the public.

discovery.text: In 1978, the US launched the New Car Assessment Program to rate crash safety publicly.

twist.text: Car companies lobbied hard against ratings, fearing bad scores would crush sales.

climax.text: Public scores created a safety arms race—brands competed for the highest star rating.

punchline.text: Public crash scores turned safety into a selling point.

quiz.question: When was the first US public crash test rating program established?

details.summary: Formal crash test programs began in the 1950s when researchers started slamming cars into barriers under controlled conditions, replacing anecdotal evidence with measurable safety data.
details.whyItMatters: Before standardized crash testing, manufacturers had no objective way to compare vehicle safety. Crash test programs gave engineers data to improve designs and gave consumers tools to choose safer cars.
takeaways: Early crash tests were conducted by universities and insurers
The first government-backed program launched in the 1970s
Standardized tests made car safety measurable and comparable

faq.question: Who conducted the first organized vehicle crash tests?
faq.answer: Universities and insurance industry labs conducted early crash tests in the 1950s. The US government formalized the program in 1978 with the New Car Assessment Program under NHTSA.

faq.question: How did early crash tests differ from modern ones?
faq.answer: Early tests used basic dummies with few sensors and simple barrier impacts. Modern tests include multiple offset configurations, side pole impacts, and dummies packed with dozens of precision instruments.
